\chapter{Numerī Ōrdinis}
\label{ch:la-ordinals}
\hlchaptermodality{55}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first, second, third, fourth and fifth in Latin, and use them to say which hour or which day I mean.}

The fifth ordinal, said against the four before it, and the month whose name it is.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[prīmus, prīma, prīmum]{prīmus — counting in order, and the word with no ūnus in it}

\label{lesson:LA-C55-primus}



\begin{quote}
A new kind of counting starts here, so the recalls come first, at the four growing distances this book measures.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pēs} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{edō} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lūdō} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{amīcus} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{prīmus, prīma, prīmum} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{first}.\textquotedblright{}

Counting does two different jobs. \emph{Ūnus, duo, trēs} answer \textbf{how many}. This word answers \textbf{which one in the line}, and Latin keeps a whole second series for that job.

Then the surprise. There is no \emph{ūnus} anywhere in \emph{prīmus}. It is a superlative of an old \emph{pri-}, \textquotedblleft{}in front\textquotedblright{} — so the word means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{foremost}\textquotedblright{}, not \textquotedblleft{}one-th\textquotedblright{}. That is why it looks nothing like the number it stands next to.

It changes its ending with the thing it counts, exactly as \emph{bonus} and \emph{malus} do: \emph{prīma hōra}, \textquotedblleft{}the first hour\textquotedblright{}; \emph{prīmus diēs}, \textquotedblleft{}the first day\textquotedblright{}.

English took the whole family: \textbf{prime}, \textbf{primary}, \textbf{premier}, \textbf{primitive} — and \textbf{prince}, from \emph{prīnceps}, \textquotedblleft{}the one who takes the first place\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prīmus, prīma, prīmum}
  \item \emph{prīma hōra} — the first hour
  \item \emph{prīmus diēs} — the first day
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question does \emph{prīmus} answer — how many, or which one in the line? (\textbf{Which one in the line}.) What number word is hiding inside it? (\textbf{None} — it is built on \emph{pri-}, \textquotedblleft{}in front\textquotedblright{}, and means \textquotedblleft{}foremost\textquotedblright{}.) And what does the ending do when the thing counted changes? (\textbf{It changes with it} — \emph{prīma hōra}, \emph{prīmus diēs}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[secundus, secunda, secundum]{secundus — the one that follows}

\label{lesson:LA-C55-secundus}



\begin{quote}
Recalls before the second ordinal, at the four measured distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{prīmus} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bibō} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{exspectō} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pecūnia} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{valē / valēte} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{secundus, secunda, secundum} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{second}.\textquotedblright{}

Like \emph{prīmus}, it is not built on its own number. There is no \emph{duo} in it. It comes from \emph{sequī}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to follow}\textquotedblright{} — so second place is the place that \textbf{comes after}, named by what it does rather than by where it falls in a count.

That single fact explains a shelf of English words. \textbf{Second} is this word, borrowed whole. So are \textbf{sequel}, \textbf{sequence}, \textbf{consequence} and \textbf{subsequent}; every one of them still carries \textquotedblleft{}follow\textquotedblright{} in it.

And the second on a clock is the same word twice over. The Romans cut the hour into small parts, \emph{pars minūta prīma}, \textquotedblleft{}the first small part\textquotedblright{} — our \textbf{minute} — and then cut that again into \emph{pars minūta secunda}, \textquotedblleft{}the second small part.\textquotedblright{} English kept the adjective and threw the noun away, so a \textbf{second} is literally \textquotedblleft{}the following one\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{secundus, secunda, secundum}
  \item \emph{secunda hōra} — the second hour
  \item the pair — \emph{prīmus, secundus}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did the root behind \emph{secundus} mean? (\textbf{To follow} — \emph{sequī}.) So what is second place, in Latin's own terms? (\textbf{The place that comes after}.) And why is a \emph{second} on a clock called that? (It is the \emph{pars minūta} \textbf{secunda} — the second cutting of the hour, after the \textbf{minute}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tertius, tertia, tertium]{tertius — where the number starts to show through}

\label{lesson:LA-C55-tertius}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the third ordinal — and the first one you can see a number inside.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{secundus} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{oculus} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{respondeō} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{medicus} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{grātiās tibi agō} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tertius, tertia, tertium} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{third}.\textquotedblright{}

Two ordinals have now gone past with no number in them at all. This one is different: \emph{trēs} is \textbf{three}, and \emph{ter-} is \emph{trēs} worn down to fit an ending. Say them together and the join is audible — \emph{trēs}, \emph{tertius}.

So the third word in the series is the first one that is built the way you would expect all of them to be built: take the number, put an ending on it, and let the ending agree with the thing counted. \emph{Tertia hōra}, \textquotedblleft{}the third hour\textquotedblright{}.

English borrowed it late and kept it formal: \textbf{tertiary}, a \textbf{tercet} (three lines of verse), \textbf{tierce}. Spanish wore it down instead of borrowing it, into \emph{tercero} — which is what happens to a word that stays in a language's mouth rather than being fetched out of a book.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tertius, tertia, tertium}
  \item the join — \emph{trēs $\to$ tertius}
  \item the three so far — \emph{prīmus, secundus, tertius}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number is inside \emph{tertius}, and what shape does it take? (\emph{\textbf{Trēs}}, worn down to \emph{ter-}.) Why is that worth noticing here rather than earlier? (\textbf{The first two ordinals had no number in them at all}.) And what did Spanish do with this word instead of borrowing it? (\textbf{Wore it down} into \emph{tercero}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quārtus, quārta, quārtum]{quārtus — the shape the rest of the series keeps}

\label{lesson:LA-C55-quartus}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the fourth — and the shape that carries the rest of the way.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tertius} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{auris} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{conveniō and occurrō} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mīles} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ita and nōn} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quārtus, quārta, quārtum} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{fourth}.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Quattuor} is \textbf{four}, and \emph{quārtus} is \emph{quattuor} with the middle squeezed out and an ending put on. After the odd pair at the front, that is the shape the series keeps: the number you already know, wearing an ending, behaving like a describing word and agreeing with whatever it counts.

Which means the first three were the hard part, and they are behind you. From here, if you can say the number you can nearly say the ordinal.

\emph{Quārta hōra}, \textquotedblleft{}the fourth hour\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Quārta pars}, \textquotedblleft{}the fourth part\textquotedblright{} — and that phrase went into English three separate times: a \textbf{quart} (a fourth of a gallon), a \textbf{quarter}, and a \textbf{quarto} (a sheet folded into four). A \textbf{quartet} is four players; a \textbf{quatrain} is four lines.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{quārtus, quārta, quārtum}
  \item the join — \emph{quattuor $\to$ quārtus}
  \item the four so far — \emph{prīmus, secundus, tertius, quārtus}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to \emph{quattuor} on the way to \emph{quārtus}? (\textbf{The middle is squeezed out} and an ending goes on.) Which of the first four ordinals do NOT have their number inside them? (\emph{\textbf{Prīmus}} and \emph{\textbf{secundus}}.) And what does the ending of \emph{quārtus} do? (\textbf{Agrees with the thing counted} — \emph{quārta hōra}, \emph{quārtus diēs}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quīntus, quīnta, quīntum]{quīntus — the fifth, and a month you have already met}

\label{lesson:LA-C55-quintus}



\begin{quote}
Recalls first, then the fifth — and a payoff from a chapter long behind you.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quārtus} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pēs} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{emō} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{epistula} — \textbf{R3}, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{avē / avēte} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{the first chapter's own recombining} — \textbf{R4}, a second word from the same distance
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quīntus, quīnta, quīntum} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{fifth}.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Quīnque} is \textbf{five}; \emph{quīntus} is that number with the ending on it, exactly as \emph{quārtus} was. Two in a row now behave the same way.

And here is where the series pays back something you were already told. The month lesson listed \textbf{Quīntīlis} among the twelve and translated it \textquotedblleft{}the fifth\textquotedblright{} — the month that was later renamed \emph{Iūlius}. You could read that translation then. Now you can see the word: \emph{Quīntīlis} is \emph{quīntus} turned into a month's name, and \emph{Sextīlis} beside it is the next ordinal doing the same.

English has \textbf{quintet} (five players), \textbf{quintuplets}, and \textbf{quintessence} — the \emph{quīnta essentia}, the \textquotedblleft{}fifth being\textquotedblright{}, which mediaeval writers put above earth, water, air and fire.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{quīntus, quīnta, quīntum}
  \item the join — \emph{quīnque $\to$ quīntus}
  \item the month — \emph{Quīntīlis}, the fifth
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What number is inside \emph{quīntus}? (\emph{\textbf{Quīnque}}, five.) What was \emph{Quīntīlis}, and what is it called now? (\textbf{The fifth month}; it was renamed \emph{\textbf{Iūlius}}.) And what is a \emph{quīnta essentia}? (\textbf{A fifth being} — the one put above earth, water, air and fire.)
\end{tcolorbox}
